extracted.intended_audience: learned readers: natural philosophers, engineers (artificers) and physicians in a medieval scholastic tradition
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted guidance and evaluative principles from a medieval natural-philosophy treatise (De Elementis) addressing projectile motion, machine design (scorpions/catapults, sieves), air/pestilence, and venoms/antidotes. The page mixes physical theory, practical engineering rules, and medical/poison‑handling advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 1: initial impulse (prima causa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first cause of violent motion is that which makes the projectile move rapidly from the start (the initial impetus imparted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong initial impulse is sufficient to produce rapid motion; machines and thrown projectiles rely on this initial violent motion. The text explains that the initial violent motion is necessary and that subsequent motion of surrounding air can augment it; one need not assume continually infinite motions if the initial impulse is adequate. Examples/analysis: projectiles launched from scorpions/machines show greater effective force when initial impulse is stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 2: magnitude of space (secunda causa — magnitudo spatii)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second cause is the magnitude (length) of the space through which the moving agent (machine, arm) acts: longer throwing arms or longer runways allow greater acceleration/effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer war engines (machinae bellicae) and longer arcs produce greater effect and longer flight; an arrow shot from a longer machine goes farther. The principle is used to justify placing war engines at half the height (semi‑orthon) when walls shake and for longer-range firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 3: rarity of the medium (tertia causa — raritas medii)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third cause is the rarity (low density) of the medium in which motion occurs: in rarer media (air) projectiles travel faster and farther than in denser media (water, earth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because motion in air is easier than in water or earth, machines that strike above water are preferred for ships; underwater targets suffer less dangerous impacts because the medium (water) weakens the impact. This principle explains why projectiles travel farther in less resisting media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 4: acuteness/sharpness of the projectile (quarta causa — acuitas teli)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth cause of rapid and sustained flight is the sharpness or pointedness of the projectile, which reduces resistance from the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharper missiles meet less obstruction and therefore are impeded less by the air, contributing to greater speed and duration of flight. This explains design choices like arrowheads and barbed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectile motion is composite (violent + natural + mixed) and approximates a parabola
rubrics_metrics.description: The trajectory of a projectile consists of three motions: the initial violent motion, a final natural motion, and an intermediate mixed motion; the path near the apex resembles a parabola rather than a perfect circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a projectile reaches its highest point it does not return by a circular arc but describes a curve approximating a parabola. The text uses this composite-motion model to account for observed flight paths and why projectiles ultimately fall by natural motion after violent impetus weakens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive entrainment of air augments projectile motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A projectile's violent motion is sustained and sometimes increased because adjacent parcels of air successively acquire motion from the projectile, so the moving medium contributes to continued motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why machines (scorpions/catapults) and thrown missiles sometimes deliver continued force: air initially set in motion by the throw tends to carry the projectile further as surrounding air is carried along. The text uses this to explain unusual ranges observed in machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerodynamic and geometry factors (wings, chord proximity, and embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity of chords/wings, the presence of vanes/alae and the geometry of parts adjacent to the shaft affect how a projectile moves and whether it embeds (infigitur) on impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If feathered parts (alae) or chords are near the shaft and interact with air, they can cause inclinations or rotations that make the missile stick into the target. The treatise analyses configurations (cuspis, alae, angulation) to explain why a spear or arrow embeds when thrown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative effect of weight and position on motion (linear distribution of gravity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which point on a thrown body is moved most depends on distribution of weight; parts nearer the center or with less weight are more readily moved in air — imparting torques and preferred directions of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reasons about points r, c, p etc. (diagrammatic reasoning) to show which parts are most strongly affected by impulse and why some parts of a body move farther than others, explaining rotations and why balls behave the way they do on impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle for scorpions/catapults and projectiles (embedding, wings, and machine placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of war machines and projectiles must consider length, wing/shaft geometry and placement (e.g., placing machines at specific distances/half‑heights) to maximize effect and to account for wall shaking, embedding, and range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendations include using semi‑orthon placements when walls are shaken, choosing longer throwing arms for greater range, and using projectile shapes (barbed points, wings) that ensure embedding. The text emphasizes empirical observation of machines (scorpions) showing surprising force due to combined effects described earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical-ease principle for suspended bodies (longer suspension easier to move)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body suspended from a longer thread or higher suspension point is easier to move and requires less force to achieve comparable displacement than when suspended lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by annulus experiments: an annulus suspended high moves more readily with less impulse. This principle explains why long pendulums or long‑suspended objects are easier to set in motion and to sustain motion with small forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieve (cribrum/pollinarium) machine design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rules for a rotating sieve machine to separate flour and bran: appropriate inclination (not too steep), division of the capsa into compartments, rotating wheel driving percussive tabella/patella, and arrangements to collect flour and bran so nothing is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: the sieve must not be overly inclined (so flour reaches the orifice without bran blocking); the capsa is divided into three (or optionally four) tiers with fine plates to receive sifted flour; a rotating wheel with a small capsule and tether activates a patella that shakes flour into the sieve FG; resulting flour, bran and dust are collected separately (MN, ML, IO). Advantages listed: reduced human labor, more complete collection of flour, less dust, less wear on the sieve than manual beating, ability to employ cheaper labourers, and cleaner product. Anti-pattern: too steep sieve causes loss or mixing with bran.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air motion, confinement and putrefaction/pestilence
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion and ventilation of air purify it; confined, stagnant air becomes putrid and produces pestilence. Conversely, airing (perflatio) and motion remove corruption and preserve things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: enclosed grain goes bad less quickly or more quickly depending on coldness and motion; closed, unmoving air in buried places preserves some things but can cause putrefaction in others; corrupt air borne from hidden places after long concealment can cause great pestilences. The text attributes plague origins and spread to corrupt air and exhalations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of venoms (origins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Venoms are classified by origin: (a) naturally occurring poisons that are immediately lethal, (b) poisons arising from putrefaction, and (c) poisons produced or concentrated by art (coctae, sublimatae, distillates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificially prepared venoms (distilled/sublimated) may be rarer but often more potent; naturally occurring venoms can be extremely lethal and sometimes regionally endemic. Distilled substances having taken on the nature of fire may gain penetrating and acuter power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five signs indicating a substance is venomous
rubrics_metrics.description: Five diagnostic signs: (1) an odor perceived in food (or foulness present), (2) manifest pains in stomach/heart/bladder, (3) sudden expectoration of blood, (4) a slow, wasting, fatal cachexia/tabes, and (5) gross immediate and irreparable change of color and state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signs can be used to infer that a food or substance is poisoned even when the poison is not directly apparent. The treatise notes that some venoms act immediately while others act slowly within variable timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties that make poisons more potent (distillation, dryness, heat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes such as distillation, heating/drying, and concentrating (sublimation) can increase the potency of a poison; dryness and the action of fire can strengthen and make venoms more penetrating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some poisons become acutely lethal after distillation or after being subjected to fire; conversely certain uses of fire or oil can extinguish or reduce some venoms depending on nature. The practitioner must know whether heat will destroy or intensify a particular poison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antidote design principles (contrariety, metallic preparations, vomit-inducing, slight warmth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective antidotes should have opposing qualities to the poison (contrarietatem), be somewhat dispersive/circulatory (diffusing), often metallic in nature or contain metallic oil, be slightly warm and digestive, and be capable of provoking vomiting or purgation to expel poison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended antidotes include theriac, Lemnian earth, laurel berries, mithridate, and medicines made from blooded animals (ciconia/stork), or metallic‑oil preparations combining sulphuric/metallic extracts, gentian, aconite (in specific preparations). Administration notes: induce vomiting or purgation (milk, whey, oil of nuts, other specific drinks); external application into arteries (illicion) is suggested by the author for strong cases, with the caveat that arterial application cannot help if the poison remains in the stomach. The antidote should not merely be bitter but have the right temperature and diffusive property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cautions and social/ethical notes about using poisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Using poisons requires secrecy and caution; few employ them because rulers hate such means, the necessary knowledge is rare, and administration in war or assassination is risky for the perpetrator (betrayal, detection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains sociopolitical reasons why few are poisoned despite existence of poisons: danger to the user, rarity of reliable practitioners, and the need for secrecy. It also counsels taking precautions and provides practical defensive measures (warming, rubbing with certain oils, avoiding contaminated places).

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic examples and empiric remedies (mice/animals, ciconia blood, oils)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical remedies: feeding or treating animals (mice) with certain substances, use of stork (ciconia) blood and certain earths (Lemnian) and mixtures (mithridatum) as protective or curative agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise reports folk and medical observations: certain animals tolerate poisons and their tissues/secretions can be used as antidotes; Lemnian earth and laurel berries are cited among curatives; mixtures with oil and metallic ingredients are recommended. The author stresses experience and that no single remedy is universally certain.
